The Foundation for Partnership Initiatives in the Niger Delta and the School of Media and Communication, Pan-Atlantic University, have launched a six-month media fellowship aimed at promoting evidence-based development journalism and broadening coverage of the Niger Delta. The organisations, in a statement on Friday, said the programme—known as the PIND Media Fellows Programme for Narrative Change in the Niger Delta—will provide participating journalists with specialised training, field exposure, editorial mentorship, and access to development evidence and communities across the region. According to the statement, the inaugural cohort comprises six journalists, editors, and media storytellers who are expected to produce independent reports examining solutions, innovation, enterprise, partnerships, and measurable development outcomes in the Niger Delta. The foundation disclosed that the fellowship commenced with a five-day residential Impact Journalism Academy held between November 2 and 6 at the School of Media and Communication in Lagos. The training covered development reporting, solutions journalism, impact storytelling, ethical interviewing, multimedia production, and evidence-based reporting. He noted that although the region’s challenges deserve honest reporting, they should not dominate its media narrative to the exclusion of efforts by communities, businesses, and development partners to address them. Daibo listed peacebuilding, agriculture, youth employment, renewable energy, and economic inclusion as some of the areas where development initiatives are making progress. Credible development reporting must remain rigorous, balanced, and accountable to the public,” he said. Also speaking, the Dean of the School of Media and Communication, Dr Ikechukwu Obiaya, stated that the partnership will equip journalists with the skills to assess the effectiveness of development interventions rather than merely report activities. “Development journalism requires more than reporting activities. Journalists must be able to interrogate evidence, understand systems, centre community voices, and determine whether interventions are producing meaningful change,” Obiaya said. He added that the partnership combines relevant skills with practical reporting tools that fellows will apply in their newsrooms and field assignments. Fellows of the programme are expected to participate in field immersion, develop reporting pitches, and receive editorial mentorship. Olufemi Adediran
